impinge

im-PINJ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To impinge is to have a negative effect on something; to intrude or encroach upon.

The new highway's noise began to impinge on the wildlife refuge just across the river.

Example

The company's aggressive new advertising strategy began to impinge on a smaller rival's territory, targeting the exact customers the smaller business had spent years building loyalty with.

The bigger company wasn't attacking directly -- it was gradually encroaching into space that belonged to someone else. That gradual intrusion into another's territory or rights is exactly what impinge describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

encroach: To encroach is to creep gradually into territory that belongs to someone else, the way weeds encroach on a garden. Impinge is about effect as much as space: something impinges when it presses in and has a negative effect on whatever it touches.

infringe: To infringe is to intrude on a specific right someone holds, often a legal one — you infringe a copyright or a treaty. Impinge is broader and softer: noise, demands, or schedules can impinge on your peace without any right being violated.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

respect: to honor and not interfere with someone's rights or space

honor: to treat someone's rights or space as important and not to be crossed

Where it sits · how serious the unwanted effect is — influence → impinge → violate

influence vs. impinge: To influence something simply means to have some sway over it, without the negative, intruding edge of impinge.

violate vs. impinge: To violate a right is a much more serious, direct breach than the gradual encroachment impinge usually describes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — im-

Prefix — im-: into, upon (Latin in-, which becomes im- before p)

Root — pinge

Root — pinge: to strike, drive, or fasten (from Latin pangere, which takes the form -pingere after a prefix)

Put it together

Put it together: Impinge comes from im- ('upon,' the form Latin in- takes before p) + pinge ('to strike or drive,' from Latin pangere) -- literally 'to strike upon,' which came to mean intruding on or encroaching against something.

Use the root in a new word: impact

Use the root in a new word: impact: The new policy had an immediate impact on how the office scheduled overtime.

Root Check

Word Choice

Impinge is usually followed by 'on' or 'upon,' and it almost always carries a negative shade -- something is intruding where it doesn't belong, even if only gradually. Compare it with flout, which describes openly and deliberately breaking a rule, while impinge is usually more gradual and sometimes unintentional.
